title: Pacing Strategy Affects the Sub-Elite Marathoner's Cardiac Drift and Performance
authors: Billat VL, Palacin F, Correa M, Pycke JR
population: Sub-elite recreational marathoners (finish 2 h 30 to 3 h 40)
findings: 215 of 280 runners (77%) were 'fallers' with a significant speed decrease appearing at about the 26th km.
Fallers had significantly lower performance (p=0.006) and higher cardiac drift (p<0.0001) than non-fallers.
Marathon performance correlated with the amplitude of cardiac drift (r=0.18, p=0.0018) but not with the increase in HR alone (r=0.01, p=0.80).
Because drift is very sensitive to running strategy, the authors recommend cardiac cost (HR divided by running velocity) rather than HR alone.
limitations: Observational; drift-performance correlation is weak (r=0.18) and its sign is not given in the abstract; drift is confounded by pacing, so high drift can reflect slowing as well as low durability; no environment data in the abstract.
implications: Use cardiac cost (HR per unit speed) rather than raw HR when judging drift; when the athlete slows late in a run, report drift as pace-adjusted and note that pacing, not fitness, may explain it.
A weak drift-performance link (r=0.18) argues against using drift alone to adjust race-pace targets.

verification.notes: Crossref (2020-02-19; article ID carries 2019 volume) and PubMed (Front Psychol 2020 Feb 19;10:3026) match.
